This question is probably one of the most inflammatory things one can ask of any anime community. However, I just finished Steins;Gate, and I can't help but wonder if the larger anime community hypes this show too much.

Don't get me wrong, S;G is has a gripping story, but something prevented me from "getting into it". I will try to articulate my thoughts here. Mainly, I'm wondering if I'm alone in thinking that S;G isn't all it's cracked up to be. From this point on, there are bound to be pretty big spoilers, so proceed at your own risk. Steins;Gate has a lot of interesting twists and turns, which I think are worth watching, even if the show isn't the pinnacle of the medium. So don't ruin it for yourself.

WARNING: Everything below this line is spoiler territory. Proceed with caution.

I just finished Steins;Gate and its OVA about an hour ago, and I can't help but feel a little let down. Everybody told me that this show was the greatest thing ever made, and I simply do not agree. Steins;Gate's story is very good. It is intricate and well-realized. However, I didn't find it to be all too original compared to other time travel media, such as the Terminator movies, or media which deal with time loops. The concept of redoing a particular timeframe over and over in order to save the world from ruin or to prevent a loved one's death is not all that original. The differences between S;G and other time travel/time loop media are superficial trappings; references to the real world, such as John Titor, SERN, and IBN. But these do not change the concept at its core. In essence, I feel that Stens;Gate is just another time travel show, and I don't understand why it's regarded so highly.

My lack of enjoyment of Steins;Gate may also speak to my personal preferences. I'm not much one for happy endings. I prefer more "realistic" (if you're a cynic, like me) stories in which not everyone can be saved. I had a problem with the Steins Gate world line, which was introduced in the home stretch of the series. It had been thoroughly established that Okabe could not save both Kurisu and Mayuri, and that was what much of my emotional investment rested on. I can identify more with a character that feels the pain of impotence, rather than one who can pull off the impossible. I enjoy shows in which one is confronted with one's own lack of power, not shows where the hitherto unachievable is placed within grasp by deus ex machina.

That said, I'm not completely against Steins;Gate having a happy ending, but Okabe's pain was not developed enough for me to accept that. Such an improbable ending needs to be won through excruciating pain and at great cost. Okabe did experience these two things, but the only time that I could fully grasp his despair was when he stabbed Kurisu. Before then, I could see his pain, but I was not able to feel it. I do not believe that the writers did an adequate job of conveying his inner struggle. Because of this, Okabe appeared too strong for me to identify with, and he didn't feel human at times. Of course, he was broken by witnessing Mayuri's death so many times, which would have made him impersonal. The characters comment on ths. However, I feel that this brokenness did not make sense in combination with his indomitable drive to save Mayuri.

I want to know if I missed some key aspect of this show that makes it so appealing to the anime community. Or is it just a fact of me not being into this show? It's all well and good for it to be the latter, but I want to at least try to understand. I did enjoy the show. I rated it a seven out of ten, which is a pretty good score on my scale. It is not, however, something that I would purchase, which is an indication of my truly enjoying an anime. The story is good and most of the characters are well-developed. But I do not believe that Steins;Gate is worthy of as high of praise as it receives.

[…]grandfather paradox, as Okabe would not have gone back in time had he not seen Mayuri die[…]

The way that the show dealt with this was with the multiple-timeline method: Mayuri dies in timeline A, so a message is sent from timeline A to timeline B (creating timeline B in the process). Whether or not the message would have been sent in timeline B is irrelevant, as the message came from timeline A, which is immutable.

Honestly, the way this show handled time-travel and paradoxes and all that is the closest thing I've ever seen to something plausible. They really did well on it, I thought - they covered all the issues that normally bug me when watching shows involving time travel.

Well, given the explanation of the attractor field and the convergence of certain events between "closer" timelines, the grandfather paradox isn't exactly swept away because the event to which the Beta world lines converge is Mayuri's death. Every one of the converging world lines can be seen as a backward divergence from that point (since this future event leads to changing the past), marking her death as the cause and not the effect. The VN does cover that from what I recall.

Yeah, as for the attractor field itself, it wasn't a perfect plot device.. why does it exist? What caused it? It did seem a little odd.

BUT - it's still the best implementation of time travel I've ever seen. For all the issues it did have, it still handled all the paradoxes as well as they could realistically be handled, and much better than I've ever seen them handled in any other movie or show.

You can tell the writers really tried to make something plausible, and the fact that their success was arguable (as opposed to purely "suspend your disbelief"-mode) speaks volumes for the quality of their attempt.

S;G is so highly regarded by the masses because of the mémés ("El Psy Congroo"), those real-world references, distinctive characters and its established reputation as a mainstream entry title. There also isn't really much to 'look into' for the series since most of the conflict is apparent at the surface level, making it easily accessible. That factor of simplicity plays the largest part in most people's rating of anime (and perhaps most media): One need only look at /r/anime's "discussion" of Mawaru Penguindrum whenever it's brought up, only grazing the "cute" aspect of the penguins and not their thematic significance.

This was one of my favorite anime back when I was introduced to the medium, but looking back it doesn't really stand out as anything more than a successful implementation of already-established archetypes. My largest problem would be Mayuri, the most unrealistically characterized of the entire cast. From my perspective the series is indeed overrated, though that's largely due to most viewers' lack of experience with more masterful/original executions of time travel and/or unwillingness to accept a true dilemma instead of being presented with such a deceptive dichotomy.

Oh, NVMe! You Atko, you! I was so confused.

For those wondering, NVMe is a cool transfer protocol for SSDs over PCI express. On the other hand, all SSDs (that use NVMe, SATA or otherwise) are nonvolatile memory, or NVM.

I use computers everyday...and tech savvy and have built a pc....but I am no programmer and I want to know just what this means.....that we can write and read from a hard drive 6times faster.....what about "ram"...(see I don't know much)....but will that mean it can run or operate 6x faster as well? And what about immediate potential for graphics card power ...real useable power?

Thanks for the info!!

Note that generally, this sort of thing isn't really in the realm of what a programmer is trained to deal with.

First, take a look at this extremely crude and oversimplified diagram of a PC's architecture I found via Google image search. Now take a look at this somewhat more complex diagram clearly designed by a particular technology company. In both of these you can see that one way to describe the way a PC (or a modern video game system) is built is with set of devices connected via a set of information paths, or buses. Often times, because of how these machines work, you can't have certain devices connected directly to each other. Instead, you have to have other intermediary devices, such as what people call a "north bridge" or "south bridge." Never mind why they're called this or what they do in the technical sense, just know that since different devices work at different rates and can deliver data at different speeds, these pieces sit in the middle and help direct traffic. One such traffic lane in modern computers in the PCI Express bus.

The technology described in the article has nothing to do with the handling or processing of graphics, or graphics cards, or anything of the sort (with exception to how, say, a texture file exists in your storage device and with this technology can be loaded faster). It is merely incidental that we use PCI Express for our graphics cards and that in the article they're talking about PCI Express for SSDs, so try not to get them mixed up.

Ultimately, the take away is that we're starting to make SSDs interface directly with the PCI Express bus, which means better throughput and faster SSD access times. This is good because classically, for one reason or another, and generally in larger scale server type setups and not home personal PCs, disk access times are a huge bottleneck that limit performance, forcing the people who use them to come up with clever work arounds that generally come at a price. Therefore, if you're a server designer or administrator, this is really awesome. If you're a home PC user or hardcore console gamer, it's just really interesting, but nothing to get super duper excited about.
